how: For a rectangular slab, pad or footing, convert length, width and thickness to the same unit, then multiply them. If dimensions are in feet, the result is cubic feet. Divide cubic feet by 27 to convert to cubic yards. For a project with several separate pours, calculate each section and add the volumes.
example: A slab 12 ft long, 10 ft wide and 4 in thick has a thickness of 4 ÷ 12 = 0.333 ft. Its volume is 12 × 10 × 0.333 = about 40 cu ft, or 40 ÷ 27 = about 1.48 cu yd before any ordering allowance.
tips: Measure the finished pour dimensions, not just the excavation. Check slab thickness at several locations because small depth changes affect the total volume.
Split L-shaped or irregular pours into rectangles, calculate each section, then add the results. Avoid counting overlapping sections twice.
The result is geometric volume. Discuss an allowance for uneven subgrade, form movement, spillage and delivery minimums with the concrete supplier or contractor.

how: First calculate the required concrete volume. Divide that volume by the yield per bag stated on the exact mix and bag size you plan to buy, then round up to a whole bag. Keep the volume and yield units identical. The calculator's bag yield is an input, not a universal property of all concrete mixes.
example: A 10 ft × 10 ft slab at 4 in thick contains 10 × 10 × (4 ÷ 12) = 33.33 cu ft. If the selected product label states a yield of 0.60 cu ft per bag, 33.33 ÷ 0.60 = 55.55, so the base estimate rounds up to 56 bags before any project allowance.
tips: Use the yield printed on the current bag or manufacturer's product sheet. Bag weight alone does not establish yield because mix formulations and product types differ.
For larger pours, compare the delivered ready-mix quote with the cost and labor of mixing many bags. Check access, minimum delivery quantities and placement time.
Keep unopened spare bags dry and follow the product instructions for water quantity, mixing, placement and curing.

how: Multiply the measured area length by width by the planned finished layer depth. Convert all three measurements to the same length unit before multiplying. To convert cubic feet to cubic yards, divide by 27. For multiple areas or different layer depths, calculate each separately and add the volumes.
example: A 20 ft × 10 ft driveway section with a 3 in layer uses 3 ÷ 12 = 0.25 ft depth. The geometric volume is 20 × 10 × 0.25 = 50 cu ft, equal to about 1.85 cu yd before supplier or compaction adjustments.
tips: Decide whether the specified depth is the loose delivered depth or the compacted finished depth. They are not interchangeable.
Gravel type, particle size, moisture and compaction change bulk density. If ordering by weight, ask the supplier for the density or conversion used for that exact product.
For a sloped or irregular area, divide the site into smaller sections and measure representative depths rather than assuming one uniform layer.

how: Multiply the garden area dimensions by the planned mulch depth.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft bed with a 0.25 ft depth needs 50 cubic feet of mulch.
tips: Confirm the depth recommended for the type of mulch you use.
Account for settling if appropriate to the product.

how: Add the wall or ceiling areas to be painted, subtract large openings if you have measured them, then divide the paintable area by the coverage rate on the product label. Multiply by the number of coats. The result is the estimated volume or number of coverage units, depending on the units entered.
example: For 600 sq ft of paintable wall area, product coverage of 350 sq ft per gallon and two coats: 600 ÷ 350 × 2 = 3.43 gallons. If the product is sold in one-gallon containers, plan on at least 4 gallons, subject to the surface and application method.
tips: Use the coverage rate for the exact paint, primer and surface condition. Label coverage is usually a guide, not a guarantee.
New drywall, bare plaster, porous masonry, dark color changes and textured surfaces may need primer or additional coats. Follow the coating manufacturer's system recommendations.
Measure each wall separately where heights differ. Include ceilings, trim or doors only if you intend to use the same product on them.

how: Calculate the floor area by multiplying room length by width, then multiply by 1 plus the waste percentage divided by 100. For rooms that are not rectangular, split the floor plan into simple shapes and add their areas. The waste allowance covers cutting and layout losses, not a measurement error.
example: A rectangular room 18 ft × 14 ft has an area of 252 sq ft. With a selected 10% cutting allowance, 252 × 1.10 = 277.2 sq ft of flooring to plan for. Compare this with the package coverage and round up to whole packs.
tips: Use the waste guidance from the flooring manufacturer or installer. Plank direction, diagonal layouts, room shape, product length and the number of doorways affect offcuts.
Check whether the package coverage is stated in square feet or square metres and whether it represents net installed coverage.
Keep spare material from the same production batch when practical. Dye lots, finish and product dimensions can vary between batches.

how: Calculate the total floor or wall area, then divide by the area covered by one tile. Multiply by 1 plus the selected waste percentage divided by 100 and round up to a whole tile. Make sure project area and tile area use compatible units. For several tile sizes or patterns, calculate each area separately.
example: A 240 sq ft area using 12 × 24 in tiles has tiles covering 2 sq ft each. With 10% waste: 240 ÷ 2 × 1.10 = 132 tiles. If tiles are sold by the box, divide by the stated tiles per box and round up again.
tips: Use the actual tile dimensions and package coverage. Nominal dimensions, grout joints and actual coverage can differ.
Choose a waste allowance based on room shape, diagonal or patterned layouts, tile size, cuts and installer guidance rather than assuming one percentage fits every job.
Order enough from one batch for the full project and retain spare tiles for future repairs.

how: For a rectangular room, estimate wall area as 2 × (room length + room width) × wall height. Divide by the area of one sheet and round up. This basic estimate does not deduct doors or windows and does not include a ceiling unless you add that area separately.
example: A 20 ft × 15 ft room with 8 ft walls has a wall perimeter of 2 × (20 + 15) = 70 ft. Wall area is 70 × 8 = 560 sq ft. A 4 ft × 8 ft sheet covers 32 sq ft, so 560 ÷ 32 = 17.5 and the base estimate is 18 sheets before layout and cutting allowance.
tips: Measure wall height in each area and account for partitions, closets, soffits and other surfaces that need board.
Sheet orientation, framing layout, openings, ceiling work, damaged edges and local board sizes change the final count. A sheet layout plan is more accurate than area alone.
Choose board type and thickness for the room and applicable fire, moisture, acoustic and installation requirements. This quantity estimate does not specify a compliant assembly.

how: Calculate board feet as thickness in inches multiplied by width in inches multiplied by length in feet, divided by 12, then multiply by quantity.
example: A 2 by 6 board that is 8 ft long contains 8 board feet.
tips: Use actual dimensions when pricing rough or surfaced lumber.
Supplier pricing may use different grading and measurement conventions.

how: Multiply the required quantity by the price per matching unit. If you select a waste percentage, multiply the material subtotal by 1 plus that percentage divided by 100. Confirm that the quantity unit and quoted price unit match, such as square metres with price per square metre.
example: A project needs 120 units of material at $8 per unit. The material subtotal is 120 × $8 = $960. With an 8% quantity allowance, the estimate is $960 × 1.08 = $1,036.80 before tax, delivery, labor or other charges.
tips: Use a current quote for the exact product, grade, size, finish and purchase unit. Compare like-for-like prices rather than package prices alone.
This estimate applies the waste percentage to material quantity and cost. It does not automatically include tax, delivery, labor, tools, disposal, discounts or minimum order fees.
For a budget, list uncertain items separately and compare supplier quotes with the same units, specification and delivery terms.

how: Calculate the paved area and divide it by the face area of one paver. Multiply by 1 plus the selected waste percentage divided by 100, then round up to a whole paver. Use the actual face dimensions and compatible area units. This is a surface coverage estimate and does not calculate the excavation, base, bedding sand or edge restraints.
example: A 16 ft × 12 ft patio is 192 sq ft. A 12 × 6 in paver covers 0.5 sq ft. With 5% cutting allowance: 192 ÷ 0.5 × 1.05 = 403.2, so the base order estimate is 404 pavers before rounding to full packs.
tips: Paver dimensions can be nominal. Confirm the manufacturer's actual dimensions and coverage per pack, including joint spacing if specified.
Herringbone, curves, borders, soldier courses and edge cuts can use more material than a simple rectangular running layout.
A paver surface needs a suitable base, bedding layer, drainage and edge restraint. Those quantities and design requirements are outside this calculator.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 20 ft by 10 ft area with a 0.1 ft layer needs 20 cubic feet.
tips: Confirm the planned layer depth and whether the supplier sells loose or compacted material.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 10 ft by 10 ft bed with a 0.5 ft depth needs 50 cubic feet of soil.
tips: Account for settling and the finished grade when choosing an order quantity.

how: Convert fence length to inches and divide by the picket width plus the gap, then round up.
example: A 100 ft fence with 5.5 inch pickets and a 1.5 inch gap needs 172 pickets in this simplified straight-run calculation.
tips: Check the actual picket width and desired spacing before ordering.

how: Divide fence length by planned post spacing, round up, then add one post for the starting position.
example: A 100 ft fence at 8 ft spacing requires 14 posts.
tips: Corners, gates and ends can require additional posts.

how: Estimate the number of board rows from deck width and board width plus gap, then divide the deck length by board length and add waste.
example: A 12 ft by 20 ft deck using 6 inch boards, a 0.125 inch gap and 12 ft boards needs 48 boards before waste in this simplified row calculation.
tips: Joins, overhangs, picture framing and board lengths can change the actual quantity.

how: Divide roof surface area in square feet by 100.
example: A 2,400 square foot roof surface equals 24 roofing squares.
tips: Use measured roof surface area when available. A roofing square is 100 square feet.

how: Start with the measured roof surface area, not the building footprint. Multiply the roof area by 1 plus the selected waste percentage divided by 100. If you only know the plan footprint, each roof plane must be measured or adjusted for its pitch before using this calculator.
example: If the combined measured roof planes total 1,800 sq ft and the chosen project allowance is 12%, the estimated material area is 1,800 × 1.12 = 2,016 sq ft. Convert that area to bundles or packages using the coverage stated for the exact roofing product.
tips: Measure each roof plane and include dormers, valleys, hips and other details. A footprint area alone understates a pitched roof's surface area.
Waste depends on roof shape, pitch, shingle or panel dimensions, pattern, starter and ridge products, and installer practice. Follow the roofing system manufacturer's estimating guidance.
Underlayment, flashing, drip edge, fasteners, ventilation and accessories are separate items unless explicitly included in the product coverage.

how: Multiply volume by the bulk density expressed in compatible units.
example: If 10 cubic units of gravel have a bulk density of 1.6 weight units per cubic unit, the estimate is 16 weight units.
tips: Use the supplier's stated density for the specific material.

how: Multiply concrete volume by the density expressed in compatible units.
example: If 10 cubic units of concrete have a density of 150 weight units per cubic unit, the estimate is 1,500 weight units.
tips: Use a density compatible with the volume units you entered.

how: Multiply length, width and depth using the same unit for all dimensions.
example: A 20 by 1 by 0.5 unit footing has a volume of 10 cubic units.
tips: Use the planned footing dimensions from the project design.
Add allowances only when appropriate to the project.

how: Multiply the number of bars by the length of each bar.
example: 20 bars at 4 units each require 80 length units.
tips: This is a length estimate and does not account for laps, hooks or cutting.
Use the bar schedule for final ordering.

how: Divide required gravel volume by the coverage of one bag and round up.
example: 10 cubic units divided by 0.5 cubic units per bag requires 20 bags.
tips: Use the actual bag coverage printed by the supplier.
Account for compaction where relevant.

how: Divide total measured baseboard length by the length of one piece and round up.
example: 100 units divided by 8 units per piece requires 13 pieces.
tips: Measure around the actual room perimeter.
Subtract openings only when they will not receive baseboard.

how: Divide wall area by the coverage of one roll and round up.
example: 120 square units divided by 25 square units per roll requires 5 rolls.
tips: Use the manufacturer's coverage and pattern information.
Pattern repeats and waste can increase the required rolls.

how: Divide total vertical rise by the planned riser height and round up.
example: A 96 unit total rise at 8 units per riser gives 12 risers.
tips: Use the final stair design for code-compliant dimensions.
This is a quantity estimate, not a stair design tool.

how: Multiply length by width by depth using consistent units.
example: A 20 by 10 area at 0.2 depth requires 40 cubic units of asphalt.
tips: Use the planned compacted depth where appropriate.
Supplier conversion and density may be needed for ordering by weight.

how: Multiply length, width and depth, then divide cubic feet by 27 when the inputs are in feet.
example: A 27 by 1 by 1 foot volume equals 1 cubic yard.
tips: Use feet for all three inputs when using this conversion.
For ordering, confirm supplier conventions and compaction.

how: Multiply length by width using the same unit for both measurements.
example: A 20 by 15 rectangle has an area of 300 square units.
tips: Use the actual finished dimensions.
Irregular areas may need to be split into multiple rectangles.

how: Multiply length by width by height using consistent units.
example: A 20 by 15 by 2 rectangular volume is 600 cubic units.
tips: This tool assumes a rectangular shape.
Use consistent units for all dimensions.
